demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The event happened because of the way I acted
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Triggers: Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'accidentally caused serious injury to another', the trigger set is clinically incoherent. All three triggers are positively valenced interpersonal cues (affection, praise, positive emotion) with no trauma-specific or guilt-linked cue; as a trio they are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and with this trauma type, where reminders of responsibility, injury, driving/scene cues, or criticism are more plausible. While one such item could occur idiosyncratically, all three together are implausible.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I am permanently an outsider now' is a poor fit with the rest of the profile and trauma type. The other appraisals center on guilt and diminished capability, which fit accidental injury, but a stable outsider/alienation identity is not well supported by the selected triggers or memory items and is more characteristic of chronic interpersonal trauma or stigmatized victimization. This creates a cross-node mismatch rather than a coherent guilt-based formulation.

vignette:
Priya

Priya had been teaching eighth-grade mathematics for seven years, and her colleagues called her the best in the department. She had a gift for breaking down complex concepts, for catching the moment a student's confusion shifted into understanding. She stayed late most afternoons, setting up experiments, grading papers with detailed feedback, planning lessons that made algebra feel alive. That was who she had been before the accident—someone capable, someone her students trusted.

It happened on a Tuesday in March, during a field trip to the botanical gardens. Priya was leading a group of twenty students through the greenhouse section, explaining photosynthesis, when she turned sharply to point out a particular specimen. Her elbow caught the edge of a glass display case—one that was supposed to be secured but had come loose over time. The case fell directly onto Marcus, a quiet boy in the back row. His arm shattered in two places. The sound of the glass breaking and his scream are still vivid to her, rendered in snapshot clarity: Marcus on the ground, his face contorted, the strange angle of his arm, her own hands trembling. When she closes her eyes, she can smell the warm, humid air of the greenhouse mixed with something metallic and sharp.

In the weeks that followed, Priya told herself it was an accident. The school's investigation confirmed it. But the distinction between accident and responsibility had become meaningless to her. She had turned carelessly. She had not checked the case. She had been the adult in charge. What had happened was a direct result of her own negligence, her own failure to maintain the careful awareness that a teacher must hold. She had come to believe that she was no longer capable of the thing that had defined her—that the person who could be trusted with other people's children no longer existed. This conviction that she was fundamentally negligent and untrustworthy meant that ordinary moments in her teaching life—a student asking a question, a colleague mentioning the field trip, even praise for her work—began to feel like potential confirmations of her incompetence, each one a hidden threat she had to interpret and survive.

The memory intrudes without warning, and when it does, it feels present rather than past. She will be sitting at her desk during her planning period, and suddenly she is back in that greenhouse, the smell of soil and glass in her nostrils, watching Marcus fall. The sensation is so immediate that her heart rate spikes and her hands grow cold. These moments pull her back so forcefully that she loses several minutes to the conviction that it is happening again, right now.

When her principal called her into his office three weeks into the new school year to praise her work with a struggling student—a girl who had finally grasped fractions—Priya felt something inside her fracture. Because she had already concluded that she was a danger to her students, the praise itself became evidence that she was deceiving people, masking her true nature; her appraisal that she was fundamentally untrustworthy transformed what should have been a moment of reassurance into a trigger for the very memory she feared most. The praise was meant to reassure her, to signal that she had not lost her competence. Instead, it triggered the memory with brutal intensity. If she was being praised now, it meant she was fooling people into thinking she was still capable, still trustworthy. The compliment itself became evidence of her deception. That night, unable to sleep, she found herself replaying the moment: the praise, the smile on her principal's face, and then—unbidden—the greenhouse, the glass, Marcus screaming. The two moments had become entangled in her mind, the positive attention and the remembered trauma locked together.

She began to avoid situations where she might receive recognition. She stopped staying late. She submitted only the minimum required lesson plans. When a parent emailed to thank her for her patience with their son, Priya felt her chest tighten. When colleagues mentioned the field trip casually—someone asking if she'd seen Marcus's recovery updates, or suggesting a new greenhouse visit—the memory would surface immediately, vivid and present, carrying with it the smell, the sound, the conviction that she had caused irreparable harm through her own recklessness.

By November, Priya had become someone her colleagues barely recognized. She was quieter, more distant. She had also come to see herself as permanently outside the community she had once felt part of—no longer one of the good teachers, no longer someone worthy of trust or connection. Her husband noticed her withdrawing, the way she would tense when he tried to touch her, the way she had stopped talking about work entirely. When he suggested she might benefit from speaking to someone, she made an appointment, not out of hope but out of a desperate need to understand why she could no longer be the person she had been, and whether that person could ever be recovered.
